sections.report:
**Section.** The whole piece: applies.

**Findings**
1. None of the checklist lines in this section is answered no. The one finding comes from reading the copy, which the checklist has no line for. **The times are too vague for a reader to plan a trip.** In the body copy (about x 120–850, y 175–400), "every forty minutes between early morning and late evening" gives no first or last sailing. "In winter the timetable thins to one boat each hour" doesn't say which months count as winter. The last paragraph then sends the reader to "the shelter at each landing" for a printed timetable. So a reader on this page still can't answer the question they came with: "When can I catch a boat, and when is the last one back?" The only way to find out is to go to the landing. Departure times and season dates are what people act on and later hold the operator to, so vague wording there is a defect, not a matter of style. Fix: give the first and last departures from each landing (for example "first boat 6:20 from the north landing, last 22:40 from the market quay"), give the winter months, and link to the timetable or put it on the page instead of only pointing to the shelter. Defect. Weight: major. This judgement is common sense about copy, not a published rule.

**What's working.**
- **One clear subject.** The small grey "PASSENGER NOTES" label, the bold "Before you board" headline and three short paragraphs read as one practical notice within seconds. There is no decoration, and every element does a job: the label tells you what kind of page this is, and the headline tells you when to read it.
- **Plain, consistent styling.** One typeface, near-black on white, the same spacing between paragraphs and a single left edge make it feel calm and trustworthy, which suits a public-transport notice.

**Checklist.** The whole piece: 8 lines, 8 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Walk (working notes).** First read: the eye lands on "Before you board" (about x 120–420, y 108–148), notices the small grey "PASSENGER NOTES" label above it, then moves down into three short paragraphs. It reads as a passenger information block for a river ferry, and it feels calm and plain. Assumed job: a web or info-page section that tells foot and bicycle passengers what to expect before boarding.
- Does one element stand clearly above the rest? **yes**
- Can you tell each level of the text from the next at a glance? **yes** (three sizes: about 13 px caps label, about 40 px title, about 18 px body)
- Where headings are larger, do they also differ in weight, form, or color? **yes**

No line came out `no` or `unsure`, so I had no entries to open.

**Section.** What matters first (hierarchy): applies.

**Findings**
None.

**What's working.**
- The title "Before you board" (about x 120–420, y 108–148) is the only large element on the page. It looks to be about twice the body size, it is bold, and it is the darkest text, so the eye knows where to start straight away. Nothing else on the page competes with it.
- Each level differs in more than one way. The "PASSENGER NOTES" label (y ≈ 83) is small, all caps, letterspaced, bold and grey. The title is large, bold and near-black. The body is mid-size, regular weight and dark grey. Because every step changes size together with weight, form or colour, no two levels can be confused, and the label reads as a category tag rather than a second headline. Keep these three distinct treatments if the piece is revised.

**Checklist.** What matters first: 3 lines, 3 yes, 0 no, 0 unsure

**Section.** Arrangement and space: applies.

**Findings**
1. **Does the visual weight balance, with no side, crowded or empty, that makes the page look about to tip?** No. All the content sits in the upper-left. It fills a block from about x=120 to x=850 and from y=75 to y=400, which is roughly 57% of the width and the top half of an image about 1280×800. Nothing sits in the right third (x≈870 to 1280) or the lower half (y≈410 to 800). Looked at as a whole frame, the page tips up and to the left, and the empty space below reads as "the page ran out" rather than as a resting area. That's because the text block has no counterweight: no rule, image, timetable, footer or anchor at the bottom (Arnheim, *Art and Visual Perception*, ch. I "Balance": a heavy side needs a counterweight). This is fine if the capture is one screen of a longer page, or if the column sits beside navigation or a sidebar in the real layout, and I can't tell which from this image. If this really is the whole page, give the lower area a job. The usual way is to set the content that the copy already points to (the crossing times, the winter timetable, where to find printed timetables) as a second block on the same x=120 column, or as a block in the right third. The other option is to anchor the bottom with a footer so the empty area reads as chosen. Mostly taste with a convention behind it. Weight: minor. The text reads fine as it is, and the cost is only that the page looks unfinished.

**What's working.** Every element starts on the same left edge, x=120: the kicker, the heading and all three paragraphs. There are no near-misses, so the page reads as one column placed on purpose (Müller-Brockmann, one grid). The spacing also shows the groups clearly. The kicker sits about 10 px above the heading, the heading sits about 35 px above the first paragraph, and the paragraphs are about 20 px apart. So "Passenger notes" and "Before you board" read as one label unit, and the three notes read as one body below it.

**Couldn't judge from a still.** Whether the empty lower half is the end of the page or only the end of this viewport, and how the column behaves on narrower screens. Check both in a live browser.

**Checklist.** Arrangement and space: 13 lines, 12 yes, 1 no (visual weight balances)

I've walked the text checklist and read up on line length. Here's the report.

**Section.** Text: applies.

**Findings**
1. **"Do paragraph lines run about 45 to 75 characters?"** Mostly no. The body column runs about 730 px wide (x 120–850). At roughly 18 px type, the full lines hold about 80 to 85 characters. For example, "The river ferry runs from the north landing to the market quay every forty minutes" (y ≈ 188) is about 83 characters. That's a little over Bringhurst's 45–75 range (*The Elements of Typographic Style*, 2.1.2, ideal 66). The text is short, only three paragraphs of two or three lines each, so readers can still find the start of the next line. Long lines just make it a bit more tiring than it needs to be. To fix it, narrow the column to about 600–640 px, which gives roughly 65–70 characters at this size. The right side of the page is empty anyway, so this costs nothing in layout. Convention. Weight: minor.
2. *(Copy, not a checklist line, given to the director in case it's useful.)* "every forty minutes between early morning and late evening" (y ≈ 188–214) is the one thing a passenger plans around, and it gives no first or last sailing time. Readers may each guess their own idea of "early" and "late", and someone could miss the last boat. In "In winter the timetable thins to one boat each hour" (y ≈ 362), "winter" has no dates, so readers can't tell when the change starts. The fix is to give real times and dates ("first boat 6:20, last boat 21:40"; "from November to February"), or to point to where they're listed. Defect. Weight: minor to major, depending on whether the real timetable sits next to this note.

**What's working.**
- The eyebrow "PASSENGER NOTES" is short, in tracked bold capitals and muted grey. It reads clearly as a label above the heading and doesn't compete with it, and its letterspacing keeps the capitals readable at a small size.
- The paragraphs are separated by space only, with no indent, and lines are spaced at about 1.5 (≈27 px on ≈18 px). With one face in a plain flush-left rag, the three notes are calm and easy to scan.

**Checklist.** Text: 30 lines, 29 yes, 1 no (lines of 45 to 75 characters)

**What's working.** The page is all neutrals with a clear range of light and dark. The near-black heading and body text on white carry everything, and the gray "PASSENGER NOTES" label (about x 120–272, y 76–90) sits one step lighter. That makes the label read as secondary through value alone, with no extra hue (Refactoring UI: lighter, not smaller). For a short practical notice this is the right amount of color: nothing competes with the facts. The label's gray still looks dark enough to read comfortably, though the Text section should confirm its contrast with a measurement.
